Human in the Loop (HITL) Mini Lab¶

Background: The Task and Its Challenges¶

For this lab, we will build upon previous computer vision labs and mini labs with a new dataset and a task that's directly relevant to your professor's research.

Our dataset is a random sample of scanned page images from The Comics Journal, an American magazine of news and criticism pertaining to comic books, comic strips and graphic novels published in one form or another since 1976.

Using rule-based methods (dilating, thresholding, edge detection, etc.), I converted these page images into smaller segments, each one theoretically representing "a block of content" on a page surrounded by white space. Some of these blocks are very clear chunks of magazine text, such as a paragraph or an entire column, and some of them are illustrations, advertisements, comic strips, etc. There are many things that we might think of as errors, where a partitioned shape was identified but it's actually two separate blocks or part of a larger image that wasn't recognized.

Associate Professor of Philosophy Sam Cowling and I are writing an article about The Comics Journal related to the way certain comics are discussed and analyzed, so this project is a spin-off of that work. Our goal is to sort image segments into two categories: segments where only text appears in the image, and segments where anything besides text appears, even if the image is mostly text.

Setup: The Importance of Folder Locations¶

Before we start, let's look at how your professor has set up your Github repo. (It turns out, I made some fairly specific decisions, and I had reasons for doing so.) In HITL Machine Learning, there's an emphasis on simple labeling interfaces that do the following:

  1. Cast your problems as binary choices wherever possible.
  2. Ensure that expected responses are diverse to avoid priming.
  3. Use existing interaction conventions.
  4. Allow keyboard-driven responses. (Monarch 16)

For this mini lab, we don't have time to build a web interface, but our task is simple enough that we can use our file system as a minimal labeling interface. Our unlabeled data is already divided into a train_test folder and an evaluate folder. I set aside the evaluate data before labeling it, as Monarch recommends, because "there are many ways to inadvertently bias your evaluation data after you have started other sampling techniques" (41). After selecting a small evaluate sample (n=200), I moved it to subfolders representing the labels. Since we are trying to presort the data into images of "all text" and images with anything besides text, I called my subfolders only_text_block and not_only_text_block. The rest of the images (n=1500) can be found in the train_test folder. They are unlabeled.

As you go through the images, you will "label" files by moving them to folder locations that describe their category (as I demonstrated with the Calvin & Hobbes images). You should be able to identify which category an image belongs to and move it to a new location very quickly. (I completed my initial batch of 200 in about 20 minutes).

The core of HITL of Active Learning is to use quantitative methods to decide which images to label by hand. As we do this, we will:

  1. Execute code that selects files for human labeling and moves files from the train_test folder to a temporary folder called to_label (various selection strategies are possible)
  2. Execute code that records a log of which active learning iteration we are running, which images were selected, and why each was chosen
  3. Label our to_label image by hand by moving them to the only_text_block and not_only_text_block subfolders.
  4. Retrain, retest, and reevaluate our model
  5. Record the results of the evaluation in our logfile
  6. Repeat steps 1-5 using a mix of selection strategies or the same strategy multiple times until some threshold is met (performance reaches a certain point, or X number of images are labeled)

Question 2¶

  • Describe how you would categorize each of the above image segments and explain your decisions.

I would only put the first image (February_2008_288_1003063202-i00128_7.jpg) into only_text_block because the picture only consists of a large chunk of text without any other visual elements. As such, I would put the other two images into not_only_text_block as those two images contains other elements and not just texts.

Iteration 1: Select Images¶

Since we have very few labels, we need to ask what is a big enough sample for our initial model. In our reading, the HITL example starts with 100 labeled text documents for each class label. My first pass of 200 images yielded 140 images belonging to the only_text_block class and 60 images belonging to the not_only_text_block class. A random sample of 200 more images should yield at least 100 for each class. Since we don't yet have any information about the unlabeled images, we should use random selection.

Question 3¶

  • Write a function to select 200 random images from the train_test folder and move them to the to_label folder that you created. We're moving them instead of copying them because we don't want to select any duplicates in a later iteration.
  • Your function should return a list of the image you selected so you can save it for later use
  • For convenience, call this function select_and_move_images_random()
  • Define and call your function below
In [ ]:
all_images = []

for file in os.listdir("train_test"):
    all_images.append(file)
In [ ]:
def select_and_move_images_random(count):
    sample_images = random.sample(all_images, count)
    
    for image in sample_images:
        source_path = os.path.join("train_test", image)
        destination_path = os.path.join("to_label", image)
        shutil.move(source_path, destination_path)

    return sample_images
In [ ]:
select_and_move_images_random(200)

Iteration 1: "Label" Your Selections¶

Now we need to label our 200 images. Outside of your Jupyter Notebook, open up the to_label folder and look at the images in it. On most computers, you can change your view settings from list or columns to icons or gallery so that you can see a preview of each image. As you glance at them, it should be obvious for most of them which images are all text and which images aren't. As you identify them, simply drag each image to the correct subfolder, only_text_block or not_only_text_block. If you have a hard time classifying an image, open it in Preview, Adobe, etc. and give it a closer look.

Iteration 1: Image Selection Logfile¶

Each time we select images for labeling, we will want to write some kind of logfile with information about the selection phase, like this:

image_filename actual_label selection_method

somefile.png not_only_text_block some_method
... ... ...

Iteration 1: Learn from New Data¶

Now we need to stop and estimate at our class balancing, as our next rounds of annotation will not be random samples.

Question 5¶

  • Write some code to count how many images of each class we have, and to estimate the ratio of only_text_block segments to not_only_text_block segments.
  • Lastly, how can we estimate the sampling error of this ratio? Make sure your code displays the ratio estimate and the estimated sampling error below.
In [ ]:
only_count = len(iteration_1_selection[iteration_1_selection["actual_label"] == "only_text_block"])
not_only_count = len(iteration_1_selection[iteration_1_selection["actual_label"] == "not_only_text_block"])

sample_ratio = only_count / not_only_count
sampling_error = (1 / only_count) + (1 / not_only_count)

print("\nRatio of 'only_text_block' segments to 'not_only_text_block' segments:")
print(sample_ratio)
print("\nEstimated sampling error:")
print(sampling_error)

Iteration 1: Train, Test, and Evaluate¶

Finally, we can train and test our first machine learning model.

Question 6¶

Write code below to do the following:

  1. load all the images for which we have labels
  2. set up a binary image classifier (tensorflow CNN with a sigmoid function)
  3. create a train/test split of the data
  4. train your model and test it (applying your inferred class balance)
  5. evaluate model performance by looking at the precision, recall, and f1 scores for both classes
  6. make sure your code block below prints all of your performance benchmarks
In [ ]:
model = tf.keras.models.Sequential([
    # Note the input shape is the desired size of the image 200x200 with 3 bytes color
    # The first convolution
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(32, (3,3), activation='relu', input_shape=(200, 200, 3)),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(2, 2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.25),
    # The second convolution
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(32, (3,3), activation='relu'),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(2,2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.25),
    # The third convolution
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(64, (3,3), activation='relu'),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(2,2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.25),
    # Flatten the results to feed into a DNN
    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),
    # 512 neuron hidden layer
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(512, activation='relu'),
    # Only 1 output neuron. It will contain a value from 0-1 
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')])

RMSprop = tf.keras.dtensor.experimental.optimizers.RMSprop
model.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy',optimizer=RMSprop(),metrics='accuracy')

training_set = tf.keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory(
        "to_label",
        seed=123,
        image_size=(200, 200),
        subset='training',
        validation_split=0.3,
        batch_size=5)

This kind of logfile would list every labeled image in our current setup, as well as whether it ended up in the training data vs test data and finally, for test set data, whether it was correctly categorized by our model.

Iteration 2: Select Images¶

Now it's time to see if active learning can help us "specify how you elicit training data from people and determine the right data to put in front of people when you don't have the budget or time for human feedback on all your data" (4). To make use of active learning strategies, we will create new batches of images to label based on uncertainty sampling, diversity sampling, and a bit of random chance so that "every data item still has some chance of being selected randomly and being reviewed by a human, even if none of the sampling strategies would have selected it" (44). In the book, Monarch recommends each iteration be composed of:

  • 10% randomly selected from unlabeled items
  • 80% selected from the lowest confidence items
  • 10% selected as outliers

In a batch of 200 images, we will have 25 randomly selected segment images, 25 identified as outliers, and 160 of our lowest confidence items after making predictions. To employ these three strategies, we need:

  1. a way to create a random sample of images from train_test and move them to to_label, but we already have the select_and_move_images_random function from our first iteration. We just need to make sure our function can accept a sample size as an argument since our sample size here will be 25, not 200.
  2. a way to load all the images the train_test folder, make predictions about their class labels, and move the most ambiguous 160 images to the to_label folder.
  3. a way to identify outliers in the data and move the 25 most significant outliers to the to_label folder.

def load_images_for_neural_network(fnames, batch_size):
    print(len(fnames))
    while True:
        cfns = []
        for i, p in enumerate(fnames):
            cfns.append(p)
            if len(cfns) == batch_size:
                yield load_images_keras(cfns)
                cfns = []
        if len(cfns) != 0:
            yield load_images_keras(cfns)
            cfns = []
            
def load_images_keras(image_list):
    images = []
    for i in image_list:
        this_pil = image.load_img(i, target_size = (200, 200))
        this_array = image.img_to_array(this_pil)
        c_img = np.expand_dims(this_array, axis = 0)
        images.append(c_img)
    return preprocess_input(np.vstack(images))

    # Note the input shape is the desired size of the image 200x200 with 3 bytes color

    tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(32, (3,3), activation='relu', input_shape=(200, 200, 3)),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(2, 2),

Question 13¶

Normally, we'd do a few more iterations and see where we are around the 800-1000 images mark, but this is a mini lab! Instead, let's consider an alternative method for isolating outliers in our data. One thing Monarch talks about is training a completely different model to do the same task, and then isolating the outliers from that model. Knowing what we know about scikit-learn, opencv, and tensorflow, describe an approach we could take to employ this strategy. Be specific about the kind of model, how we would define/isolate outliers, and what kinds of outliers your choice of model might find.

We can use ResNet50 as a model to convert images to representation vectors. One common model for anomaly detection is the Isolation Forest algorithm, which is available in scikit-learn. Isolation Forest is effective at identifying outliers that deviate significantly from the majority of the data points. These outliers may represent anomalies, errors, or rare events in the dataset. Thus, we can complement the predictions from the primary classification model and potentially identify instances that are difficult to classify or that exhibit unusual characteristics not captured by the primary model.

Question 15¶

Interpret your model's performance below, as well, as how it changed over the course of the lab. Were our active learning strategies successful? Why or why not?

Performance scores for iteration 1:

  • Precision score of the model: [0.45454545 0.68421053]
  • Recall score of the model: [0.45454545 0.68421053]
  • F1 score of the model: [0.45454545 0.68421053]

Perfomance scores for iteration 2:

  • Precision score of the model: [0.8125 0.93406593]
  • Recall score of the model: [0.8125 0.93406593]
  • F1 score of the model: [0.8125 0.93406593]

In iteration 1, the model's performance was relatively low in precision, recall, and F1 scores for both classes. This indicates that the model had difficulty distinguishing between the two classes and was not performing well overall. In contrast, in iteration 2, the model's performance improved significantly. The precision, recall, and F1 scores increased significantly for both classes. This means that the model became more accurate and reliable in classifying the images after implementing active learning strategies.

The active learning strategies employed in iteration 2 likely contributed to the improved performance. By selecting images for labeling based on uncertainty sampling, diversity sampling, and outliers detection, we were able to provide the model with more informative and diverse training data. This helped the model to learn more robust representations of the data and generalize better to unseen examples.

In conclusion, the active learning strategies implemented in iteration 2 were successful in enhancing the model's performance.
